Vikram Award — MP's award for excellence in a single discipline
Arjuna Award — national award, Government of India
revision_takeaways: Two MP layers: Ekalavya for lifetime sporting achievement, Vikram for a single outstanding performance of the year.

MPPSC-2019-009.correct_reasoning: Sonu Golkar, a blind cricketer from Madhya Pradesh, received the Vikram Award for 2018 in the divyang (disabled) category. The award is the state's recognition of a single outstanding performance, and his came in blind cricket at national level.

option_explanations.reason: Correct. Sonu Golkar was the 2018 Vikram Awardee in the disabled category, recognised for blind cricket.
Bheem Sonkar is not the disabled-category awardee of 2018 on the state's published list.
Pooja Vastrakar is an international cricketer from Madhya Pradesh who plays for India, but not as a 2018 disabled-category Vikram Awardee.
Harshita Tomar is a sailor from Bhopal who won an Asian Games bronze in 2018; she is not the disabled-category awardee.

key_concepts: Vikram Award — MP's award for a single outstanding performance in a year
Divyang category recognises para and blind sportspersons
Blind cricket in India is run by the Cricket Association for the Blind
revision_takeaways: State sports questions often pair an award with a category — read the category word (divyang) before matching the name.

MPPSC-2019-010.correct_reasoning: Muskan Kirar, from Jabalpur, is a compound archer. She was part of the Indian women's compound team that won a silver medal in 2018 and has won medals at Asia Cup events, including a gold in the women's compound event at Bangkok.

option_explanations.reason: Kayaking and canoeing in Madhya Pradesh are associated with the Bhopal water-sports academy and with the Narmada, not with Muskan Kirar.
Sailing is Harshita Tomar's discipline; Kirar competes with the bow, not on water.
Correct. Muskan Kirar is a compound archer, and archery is one of the sports where MP has a state academy.
Athletics in MP is represented by sprinters and throwers; Kirar's medals come from archery competitions.

key_concepts: Compound archery — uses pulleys and a release aid, distinct from recurve
Muskan Kirar — Jabalpur, compound archer, 2018 team silver
MP State Archery Academy — Jabalpur
revision_takeaways: When a sportsperson's discipline is asked, look for the state academy link first: Jabalpur archery, Bhopal water sports.

MPPSC-2019-011.correct_reasoning: The Satpura system is arranged from west to east as the Barwani hills in the west, the Mahadeo range across the centre with Dhupgarh, the highest point of Madhya Pradesh, and the Maikal range in the east towards Chhattisgarh, where the Narmada rises at Amarkantak.

option_explanations.text: Barwani hills - Mahadeo range - Maikal range
option_explanations.reason: Correct. Barwani lies in the west, the Mahadeo range runs through the middle and the Maikal range is the eastern end.

option_explanations.text: Mahadeo range - Barwani hills - Maikal range
option_explanations.reason: This puts the Mahadeo range before the Barwani hills, which reverses the western end of the sequence.

option_explanations.text: Mahadeo range - Maikal range - Barwani hills
option_explanations.reason: This places the Maikal range in the middle and Barwani in the east, reversing the whole order.

option_explanations.text: Maikal range - Mahadeo range - Barwani hills
option_explanations.reason: This starts in the east with Maikal and ends in the west with Barwani, the exact reverse of the question.

key_concepts: Barwani hills — western Satpura in Barwani and Khargone
Mahadeo range — Dhupgarh, the highest peak of MP
Maikal range — Amarkantak, source of the Narmada
revision_takeaways: West to east on the Satpura map spells B-M-M: Barwani, Mahadeo, Maikal.

MPPSC-2019-012.correct_reasoning: The Chambal is notorious for its deep ravines, called bihad locally, cut into the soft alluvium of its valley by gully erosion as the river swings across its wide flood plain. The badlands stretch across the Chambal division of Madhya Pradesh and into Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh and are the landscape of the classic dacoit films.

option_explanations.reason: The Narmada cuts a gorge through marble at Bhedaghat and flows in a comparatively narrow valley, not in badlands.
The Son flows across a plateau and forms waterfalls at Deogarh and Panna; it has no such ravine belt.
Correct. The Chambal valley is India's classic ravine landscape, produced by gully erosion of its own alluvium.
The Tapti occupies a rift valley between the Satpura and Ajanta ranges and does not develop deep ravines of this kind.

key_concepts: Gully erosion — the process that carves ravines
Bihad — the local name for Chambal badlands
Ravines stretch across Morena, Bhind and Sheopur
revision_takeaways: Chambal means three things in MP geography: ravines, dacoits and the Gandhi Sagar–Rana Pratap Sagar chain of dams.

MPPSC-2019-013.correct_reasoning: Under the 2010 renumbering, the road from Indore towards Jaipur carries the number NH-52. NH-52 runs from Sangrur in Punjab to Ankola in Karnataka and passes through Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, which is why the Indore-Jaipur stretch falls on it.

option_explanations.reason: Correct. The revised number of the Indore to Jaipur route is NH-52, part of the Sangrur to Ankola corridor.
NH-47 in the old numbering ran from Salem to Kanyakumari in the south, far from Indore.
NH-3 in the old numbering was the Agra to Mumbai road through Gwalior and Indore, and it does not head to Jaipur.
NH-46 is a different corridor and does not connect Indore with Jaipur on the state's highway map.

key_concepts: NH-52 — Sangrur to Ankola, via Jaipur and Indore
Old NH-3 — Agra to Mumbai through Gwalior and Indore
The 2010 renumbering replaced the old north-south and east-west numbering
revision_takeaways: Indore's two exam highways are NH-52 (Jaipur side) and NH-3/NH-44 (Agra side).

MPPSC-2019-014.correct_reasoning: Three different kinds of source are used for the Paramara dynasty: the Navasahasanka Charita of Padmagupta, a court epic on the life of Sindhuraja; the Prabandha Chintamani of Merutunga, a fourteenth-century Jain collection of biographical anecdotes on the Paramara and Chaulukya kings; and the Udaipur Prashasti, an inscription that records the Paramara line and the death of Bhoja.

option_explanations.reason: Navasahasanka Charita is a genuine Paramara source, but the question asks for more than one and the other two are equally valid.
Prabandha Chintamani does carry Paramara material, so this option is right by itself but incomplete.
The Udaipur Prashasti does record the Paramara rulers, so it cannot be the only correct answer.
Correct. All three sources — the Padmagupta epic, the Merutunga Prabandha and the Udaipur inscription — are used for Paramara history.

key_concepts: Navasahasanka Charita — Padmagupta, on Sindhuraja
Prabandha Chintamani — Merutunga, 14th-century Jain prose
Udaipur Prashasti — inscription of the Paramara lineage and Bhoja's death
revision_takeaways: Paramara sources come in three flavours: court epic, Jain prabandha, and temple inscription.

MPPSC-2019-015.correct_reasoning: The Tribhuvan Narayan temple inside Chittorgarh fort, also called Samiddheshwar Mahadev, was built in the eleventh century by the Paramara king Bhoja. The fort was later held by the Guhilas of Mewar, and a second inscription in the temple records its renovation under Maharana Mokal.

option_explanations.reason: Rana Pratap belongs to the sixteenth century, five hundred years after the temple was built, and is associated with Haldighati.
Raja Dhang is not the builder recorded in the temple's own inscriptions.
Correct. The inscription and the temple's style point to the Paramara king Bhoja, whose realm reached this part of Mewar.
Prithviraj Chauhan ruled at Ajmer and Delhi in the twelfth century and has no building credit at Chittor.

key_concepts: Tribhuvan Narayan / Samiddheshwar Mahadev temple, Chittorgarh
Paramara king Bhoja — 11th-century builder and author
Two temple inscriptions — Kumarpal (Solanki) and Maharana Mokal's renovation
revision_takeaways: Bhoja built beyond Malwa: Dhara was his capital, but Chittor, Ujjain and Bhopal all carry his monuments.

MPPSC-2019-016.correct_reasoning: Panna is one of Madhya Pradesh's non-operational airports, along with Khandwa and Satna. The airports that handle scheduled civil flights are Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, Gwalior and Khajuraho, some of them as civil enclaves inside air force stations.

option_explanations.reason: Khajuraho is an operational airport with scheduled flights serving the temple complex and Panna tiger reserve.
Correct. Panna's airport has no scheduled commercial operations, which places it with Khandwa and Satna in the inactive list.
Jabalpur is an operational airport and also hosts a civil enclave at the Indian Air Force station.
Gwalior is operational, with a civil enclave at the air force base and scheduled flights to Delhi and other cities.

key_concepts: Operational airports of MP — Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, Gwalior, Khajuraho
Non-operational — Panna, Khandwa, Satna
Civil enclave — civil terminal inside a defence airfield
revision_takeaways: Five fly, three do not: remember Panna, Khandwa and Satna as the dormant trio.

MPPSC-2019-017.correct_reasoning: The fourteenth Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly sat from 2013 to 2018, and its Speaker was Dr Sitasaran Sharma, who held the chair from January 2014 to January 2019. The fifteenth Assembly, elected in December 2018, chose Narmada Prasad Prajapati as Speaker.

option_explanations.reason: Pandit Kunjilal Dubey was the first Speaker of the erstwhile Madhya Pradesh Assembly in the 1950s, not of the 2014-2018 Assembly.
Ishwardas Rohani was Speaker in the previous Assembly, from 2004 to 2013.
Correct. Dr Sitasaran Sharma was Speaker of the 2013-2018 Assembly and continued in office till January 2019.
Rajendra Singh did not occupy the Speaker's chair in the 2014-2018 Assembly.

key_concepts: 14th MP Assembly — 2013 to 2018, Speaker Sitasaran Sharma
Speaker's tenure ran from 9 January 2014 to 1 January 2019
15th Assembly — Narmada Prasad Prajapati, then Girish Gautam
revision_takeaways: Assembly numbers and Speakers pair up: 13th Rohani, 14th Sitasaran Sharma, 15th Prajapati and Gautam.

MPPSC-2019-018.correct_reasoning: Justice Anshuman Singh was Governor of Rajasthan and of Gujarat, but never of Madhya Pradesh. Balram Jakhar held the office from 2004 to 2009, Rameshwar Thakur from 2009 to 2011, and Dr Bhai Mahaveer from 1998 to 2003.

option_explanations.reason: Balram Jakhar was Governor of Madhya Pradesh from 30 June 2004 to 29 June 2009 after a career as Lok Sabha Speaker.
Rameshwar Thakur was Governor of Madhya Pradesh from 30 June 2009 to 7 September 2011, after serving in Odisha and Karnataka.
Dr Bhai Mahaveer was Governor of Madhya Pradesh from 22 April 1998 to 6 May 2003.
Correct. Justice Anshuman Singh held the governorships of Rajasthan and Gujarat but never of Madhya Pradesh.

key_concepts: MP Governors — Pattabhi Sitaramayya first, then Pataskar, Reddy, Sinha, Sanjiva Reddy
Bhai Mahaveer 1998-2003, Balram Jakhar 2004-2009, Rameshwar Thakur 2009-2011
Anshuman Singh — Rajasthan and Gujarat
revision_takeaways: For 'who was not' questions on Governors, check the neighbouring states first: Rajasthan and Gujarat are the usual decoys.

sources.title: Governors of Madhya Pradesh and the 'who was not Governor' question
sources.citation: Testbook and IAS Book notes on MP Governors — Bhai Mahaveer 1998-2003, Jakhar 2004-2009, Thakur 2009-2011, Anshuman Singh Rajasthan

MPPSC-2019-019.correct_reasoning: Madhya Pradesh shares boundaries with Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh. Jharkhand lies beyond Chhattisgarh's eastern edge and has no common border with Madhya Pradesh, so it is the state that does not touch it.

option_explanations.reason: Rajasthan has the longest boundary with Madhya Pradesh, running through Jhalawar, Chittorgarh and Pratapgarh districts.
Gujarat touches Madhya Pradesh along its shortest stretch, on the western edge of Jhabua and Alirajpur.
Correct. Jharkhand does not share a border with Madhya Pradesh; Chhattisgarh lies between the two.
Maharashtra borders Madhya Pradesh across Burhanpur, Khargone and Barwani in the Nimar plain.

key_concepts: MP's five neighbours — UP, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh
Longest boundary — Rajasthan; shortest — Gujarat
Jharkhand lies beyond Chhattisgarh and shares no border with MP
revision_takeaways: MP's neighbours are the five that touch the map after 2000; Jharkhand, Bihar and Odisha belong to undivided MP's history, not to today's border.

MPPSC-2019-020.correct_reasoning: Avani Vaish was Chief Secretary of Madhya Pradesh from 2010 to 2012 and never served as Commissioner of the State Election Commission. Gopal Sharan Shukla, R. Parshuram and Dr Ajit Raizada were all State Election Commissioners in succession after the Commission was constituted in February 1994.

option_explanations.reason: Gopal Sharan Shukla was State Election Commissioner from February 2000 to August 2006.
R. Parshuram served as a Commissioner of the Madhya Pradesh State Election Commission in the sequence of office-holders.
Dr Ajit Raizada also held the post of State Election Commissioner, between the tenures of Parshuram and others.
Correct. Avani Vaish was the state's Chief Secretary, not its State Election Commissioner.

key_concepts: MP State Election Commission — constituted 1 February 1994
First Commissioner — N. B. Lohani, from 15 February 1994
Chief Secretary and State Election Commissioner are different offices
revision_takeaways: The SEC is a separate constitutional office under Article 243K, never held by the state's Chief Secretary.

MPPSC-2019-021.correct_reasoning: VIRUS is popularly expanded in computer literature as Vital Information Resource Under Siege, a backronym that describes a program which hides inside a host file and multiplies, seizing the host's resources. The expansion is a memory aid rather than a formal acronym, because virus does not stand for anything in technical documentation.

option_explanations.reason: This expansion is invented; it does not appear in any standard glossary of computer terms.
Correct. Vital Information Resource Under Siege is the accepted backronym used in Indian computer awareness books and exams.
This string is a constructed distractor that fits the letters but carries no meaning in computing.
Again a made-up expansion; no glossary defines VIRUS with these words.

key_concepts: Virus — self-replicating code that needs a host file
Backronym — an acronym invented after the word exists
Worm versus virus — worms spread without a host
revision_takeaways: Treat the VIRUS expansion as a backronym, and remember that a virus needs a host while a worm does not.

MPPSC-2019-022.correct_reasoning: A cracker is someone who breaks into systems without authorisation, destroys data, denies service to legitimate users or otherwise damages the target. The word is used precisely to separate this malicious activity from the white-hat hacker, who probes systems with permission in order to report and fix weaknesses.

option_explanations.reason: A white hat hacker works with the owner's consent and reports the weakness instead of destroying data.
Correct. A cracker is the malicious intruder who breaks in, destroys data or blocks legitimate users.
A programmer writes software; nothing in the word implies unauthorised access or damage.
A database administrator maintains databases with legitimate access rights and does not intrude on other systems.

key_concepts: Hacker — explores systems; white hat does so ethically, black hat maliciously
Cracker — breaks security for damage or gain
Denial of service — blocking legitimate users, one of the acts described
revision_takeaways: If the sentence contains words like destroy, deny or unauthorised, the answer is cracker, not hacker.

MPPSC-2019-023.correct_reasoning: The Information Technology Act, 2000 is India's first cyber law and the legal foundation for electronic commerce: it recognises electronic records and digital signatures, legalises electronic transactions and creates the framework for e-governance. It was passed in June 2000 and came into force on 17 October 2000.

option_explanations.reason: There is no Information Technology Act of 1996 in India; that year belongs to the telecom and cable regulation debate.
Correct. The Information Technology Act, 2000 is the first Indian cyber law and the legal base for e-commerce.
1998 is not the year of any IT Act; the bill was drafted in the late 1990s but enacted in 2000.
1990 predates the internet in India and has no IT legislation attached to it.

key_concepts: IT Act, 2000 — electronic records, digital signatures, cyber offences
Came into force 17 October 2000
Amended in 2008 to add sections on data privacy and cyber terrorism
revision_takeaways: One date carries the answer: India's cyber law is the IT Act, 2000, amended in 2008.

MPPSC-2019-024.correct_reasoning: Phishing, cyber stalking and identity theft are all offences because each involves deception, harassment or misappropriation through a computer resource. Online chatting is simply a means of communication over the internet and is not by itself an offence, although what is said in a chat can become one.

option_explanations.reason: Phishing is fraud by a fake message or site that harvests credentials, an offence under the IT Act.
Cyber stalking is repeated unwanted contact or monitoring through the internet, punishable as harassment.
Identity theft uses another person's personal data to impersonate them, an offence under section 66C of the IT Act.
Correct. Online chatting is ordinary communication and becomes an offence only if the content itself is criminal.

key_concepts: Phishing — deceptive messages that steal credentials
Section 66C — punishment for identity theft
Cyber stalking — harassment using electronic communication
revision_takeaways: Distinguish the medium from the act: chatting is a medium, phishing and stalking are acts.

MPPSC-2019-025.correct_reasoning: In an email address the part after the @ sign is the domain name, which identifies the mail server that holds the mailbox. In mark.sttol@ITdesk.info the local part is mark.sttol and the domain is ITdesk.info, with info being only the top-level domain.

option_explanations.reason: mark.sttol is the local part, the name of the mailbox, which sits before the @ sign.
sttol on its own is only part of the local name and not the domain.
Correct. ITdesk.info is the domain name, the part after the @ sign that identifies the mail server.
info is only the top-level domain, the last label of the domain name, not the domain itself.

key_concepts: Local part — the mailbox name before @
Domain name — the part after @, identifying the mail server
Top-level domain — the last label such as .info or .com
revision_takeaways: Split the address at @, then split the domain at the first dot: everything between them is the domain.

MPPSC-2019-026.correct_reasoning: Under section 4 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, appointments to the National Human Rights Commission are made on the recommendation of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Home Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, the Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Chairman of the Council of States, that is the Vice-President, is not a member of that committee.

option_explanations.reason: The Prime Minister chairs the selection committee, so he is a member.

option_explanations.text: Speaker of the House of the People
option_explanations.reason: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is expressly named as a member of the committee.

option_explanations.text: Leader of the Opposition in the House of the People
option_explanations.reason: The Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha is also expressly named as a member.

option_explanations.text: Chairman of the Council of States
option_explanations.reason: Correct. The Chairman of the Council of States is not on the committee; it is the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha who sits on it.

key_concepts: Section 4, Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 — selection committee
Six members: PM, Speaker, Home Minister, LoP Lok Sabha, LoP Rajya Sabha, Deputy Chairman Rajya Sabha
Vice-President is Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, ex officio
revision_takeaways: NHRC selection has no Vice-President: the Rajya Sabha's representative is its Deputy Chairman.

MPPSC-2019-027.correct_reasoning: Section 6 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 provides that the Chairperson and a Member each hold office for five years or until the age of seventy, whichever is earlier, and that a Member is eligible for re-appointment for another term of five years. Because re-appointment is expressly allowed, the statement that a Member is not eligible for re-appointment is the incorrect one.

option_explanations.text: Chairman holds office for a term of five years
option_explanations.reason: The five-year term of the Chairperson is exactly what section 6(1) provides, so this statement is correct.

option_explanations.text: Members of the Commission hold office for a term of five years
option_explanations.reason: Section 6(2) gives a Member the same five-year term, so this statement is also correct.

option_explanations.text: Member is not eligible for re-appointment for another term of five years
option_explanations.reason: Correct. This statement is false: section 6(2) expressly makes a Member eligible for re-appointment for another term of five years.

option_explanations.text: Chairperson or a Member is ineligible for further employment under Government of India or Government of any State
option_explanations.reason: Section 6(3) bars further government employment on ceasing to hold office, so this statement is correct as well.

key_concepts: Section 6, PHRA 1993 — five-year term, seventy-year age cap
Re-appointment — allowed for Members, another five-year term
Section 6(3) — ineligibility for further government employment
revision_takeaways: The NHRC's one 'not' is about re-appointment: Members may be re-appointed, they are not barred.

sources.title: Term of office of members of the National Human Rights Commission
sources.citation: Section 6 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 as reproduced in statutory compilations

MPPSC-2019-028.correct_reasoning: The Chairperson and Members of a State Human Rights Commission are appointed by the Governor of the State on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Chief Minister and including the Speaker, the Home Minister and the Leader of the Opposition of the State Assembly. The President appoints the National Commission, not the State Commission.

option_explanations.reason: Correct. Section 21 of the Protection of Human Rights Act vests the appointment of the State Commission in the Governor.
The President appoints the National Human Rights Commission; state commissions are outside that power.

option_explanations.text: Chief Justice of the High Court of the concerned State
option_explanations.reason: The Chief Justice of the High Court has no appointing role, though a former High Court judge may be Chairperson.
The Chief Justice of India is not connected with state commission appointments at all.

key_concepts: Section 21, PHRA 1993 — State Commission appointed by the Governor
State selection committee — Chief Minister, Speaker, Home Minister, LoP
National Commission — appointed by the President
revision_takeaways: Centre appoints by President, State appoints by Governor — the same pattern as in most commissions.

MPPSC-2019-029.correct_reasoning: Section 31 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 allows the State Government to specify an advocate as Special Public Prosecutor for human rights courts if the advocate has been in practice for not less than seven years. The requirement mirrors the minimum practice for a High Court judgeship tie-in used in several special statutes.

option_explanations.reason: Five years is the practice requirement in some other statutes but not in section 31 of the Human Rights Act.
Six years is not the figure used in section 31; the Act fixes a longer minimum.
Ten years is the requirement for some other appointments but is higher than the section 31 threshold.
Correct. Section 31 prescribes seven years of practice as an advocate for a Special Public Prosecutor.

key_concepts: Section 31, PHRA 1993 — Special Public Prosecutor for human rights courts
Seven years' practice — the statutory minimum
Human rights courts are set up under section 30, one for each district
revision_takeaways: Human rights courts and their prosecutors sit in one number pair: section 30 creates the court, section 31 the seven-year prosecutor.

MPPSC-2019-030.correct_reasoning: Offences under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 are made cognizable and triable summarily, and section 15 of the Act makes them non-compoundable. Enforcement is therefore in the hands of the police, with a fast summary trial, and the parties cannot buy a compromise.

option_explanations.reason: Correct. The Act makes every punishable offence cognizable and triable summarily, so this option is part of the answer.
Correct. The offences are also non-compoundable, which is the second half of the statutory description.
The offences are cognizable and not bailable in the ordinary sense, so non-cognizable is wrong.
Compounding is expressly barred, so describing the offences as compoundable is wrong.

key_concepts: Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 — earlier the Untouchability (Offences) Act
Cognizable and summarily triable
Non-compoundable — no compromise settlement between parties
revision_takeaways: Remember the trio for the PCR Act: cognizable, summarily triable, non-compoundable.

MPPSC-2019-031.correct_reasoning: SathyabamaSat is a nano satellite built by students of Sathyabama University, Chennai, with ISRO's technical support, carrying payloads to study greenhouse gases and water vapour. That makes it an academic institute satellite, whereas CARTOSAT-2B, Kalpana-1 and INSAT-2E are ISRO's own remote sensing, meteorological and communication satellites.

option_explanations.reason: CARTOSAT-2B is the seventeenth satellite of ISRO's Indian Remote Sensing series, an agency mission, not a university one.
Kalpana-1 is ISRO's first dedicated meteorological satellite, launched and operated by the space agency.
INSAT-2E is the last of the INSAT-2 series, a multipurpose ISRO satellite for telecom and broadcasting.
Correct. SATHYABAMASAT was developed by a university with ISRO guidance, which is what makes it an academic institute satellite.

key_concepts: SathyabamaSat — university nano satellite with ISRO support
CARTOSAT — remote sensing series
Kalpana-1 — meteorological; INSAT — communication and broadcasting
revision_takeaways: Academic satellites carry student/university names; ISRO's own series are named by function — CARTOSAT maps, Kalpana watches weather.

MPPSC-2019-032.correct_reasoning: Knock-knee syndrome, genu valgum, in its endemic Indian form is caused by skeletal fluorosis from drinking water with excess fluoride. The knees bend inward while the ankles stay apart, and the condition is common in the fluoride belts of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh.

option_explanations.reason: Correct. Fluoride pollution of groundwater produces skeletal fluorosis, of which knock knees is a classic sign.
Mercury poisoning causes neurological damage such as Minamata disease, not knock knees.
Arsenic in groundwater causes skin lesions and keratosis, and is a problem in West Bengal and Bihar rather than this deformity.
Cadmium poisoning produces itai-itai disease with bone pain and kidney damage, not genu valgum.

key_concepts: Genu valgum — knock knees

MPPSC-2019-071.correct_reasoning: JSP stands for Java Server Pages, a server-side technology that generates dynamic web pages by mixing HTML with Java code, which the server compiles and runs before sending the page to the browser. It complements servlets and is part of the Java EE platform.

MPPSC-2019-072.correct_reasoning: Bing is Microsoft's web search engine, launched in 2009 as the successor to Live Search. It powers search in Windows and in Microsoft Edge and is one of the few general search engines with its own index.

MPPSC-2019-074.correct_reasoning: A plotter, a printer and a monitor all produce output from a computer. A keyboard, a mouse and a scanner are input devices, so any group that contains one of them fails the 'only output devices' test.

MPPSC-2019-077.correct_reasoning: Section 5 of the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 punishes a person who, on the ground of untouchability, refuses admission to any hospital, dispensary, educational institution or hostel, or refuses to supply goods or services to a member of a Scheduled Caste. MPPSC-2019-078.correct_reasoning: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Act 33 of 1989, received assent on 11 September 1989 but came into force on 30 January 1990, the date appointed by the central government. MPPSC-2019-091.correct_reasoning: Hirdeshah was the zamindar of Hirapur in Bundelkhand and one of the leaders of the Bundela rebellion of 1842, which broke out against the land revenue and succession policies of the British. Other participants were Parichhat of Jaitpur and Madhukar Shah of Narhut.

MPPSC-2017-003.correct_reasoning: The title Raja was conferred on Ram Mohan Roy by the Mughal emperor Akbar II, who was impressed by his erudition and sent him to England as his envoy. The title thus came from the Mughal court in Delhi, not from a British figure, which is why Robert Clive and the other options are wrong.

option_explanations.reason: Aurangzeb died in 1707, long before Ram Mohan Roy was born in 1772.
Clive was an East India Company officer of the mid-eighteenth century and never conferred Indian titles on reformers.
Gandhi was born in 1869 and belonged to a later generation; the title predates him by decades.
Correct: Akbar II gave Ram Mohan Roy the title of Raja and later sent him to Britain as his representative.

key_concepts: Ram Mohan Roy: Brahmo Sabha 1828, anti-sati campaign
Akbar II was the penultimate Mughal emperor (1806–1837)
Ram Mohan Roy died in Bristol in 1833
revision_takeaways: Two Akbars: Akbar the Great ruled 1556–1605, Akbar II gave Roy his title.

MPPSC-2017-004.correct_reasoning: The Indian Councils Act of 1909, the Morley-Minto reforms, introduced separate electorates for Muslims by legalising communal representation in the imperial and provincial legislative councils. Decentralisation is associated with the 1919 Act's provincial subjects and dyarchy, and legislative councils existed from 1861, so separate electorate is the defining feature of 1909.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the 1909 Act legalised separate electorates for Muslims, the step that made communal representation a constitutional rule.
Decentralisation and the division of subjects into central and provincial lists belong to the Government of India Act 1919.
Dyarchy, with transferred and reserved provincial subjects, was introduced in the provinces by the 1919 Act, not 1909.
Legislative councils were already enlarged by the Indian Councils Act 1861 and 1892, so they cannot be the mark of the 1909 Act.

key_concepts: 1909: Morley-Minto reforms, separate electorates
1919: Montagu-Chelmsford, dyarchy in provinces
1935: provincial autonomy and dyarchy at the centre
revision_takeaways: Key the three acts to one word each: 1909 separate electorate, 1919 dyarchy, 1935 autonomy.

MPPSC-2017-005.correct_reasoning: At the Battle of Chandawar, fought in 1194 on the banks of the Yamuna near Etawah, Muhammad Ghori defeated Jaichand of Kannauj of the Gahadavala dynasty, which left the Ganga-Yamuna doab open to him. Kumarpal of Gujarat, Govindraj of the Chahamana line and Bhim II of Gujarat belong to other struggles.

option_explanations.reason: Kumarpal was a Chaulukya king of Gujarat in the twelfth century, with no part in the Chandawar battle.
Correct: Jaichand of Kannauj was the Gahadavala ruler whom Ghori defeated at Chandawar in 1194.
Govindaraja was a Chahamana prince of Ajmer whose struggle was with Prithviraj Chauhan, not Ghori.
Bhimdev II ruled Gujarat and fought Ghori at Kasahrada and Mount Abu, not at Chandawar.

key_concepts: Ghori's campaigns: Tarain 1191 and 1192, Chandawar 1194
Gahadavala dynasty of Kannauj, capital Varanasi
Chandawar is near Etawah, not Farrukhabad
revision_takeaways: Ghori's three victories in order: Tarain 1192 over Prithviraj, Chandawar 1194 over Jaichand.

MPPSC-2017-006.correct_reasoning: Counting the five houses of the Delhi Sultanate, the Khilji dynasty lasted the least, from 1290 to 1320, roughly thirty years, against about eighty-four for the Mamluks, ninety-four for the Tughlaqs, thirty-seven for the Sayyids and seventy-five for the Lodis. The Sayyids come close but still outlast the Khiljis by a few years.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the Khiljis ruled from 1290 to 1320, about thirty years, the shortest span of the five dynasties.
The Tughlaqs held Delhi from 1320 to 1414, about ninety-four years, one of the longest spans.
The Sayyids ruled from 1414 to 1451, about thirty-seven years, which is short but longer than the Khiljis' thirty.
The Lodis ruled from 1451 to 1526, about seventy-five years, ending only with Babur's victory at Panipat.

key_concepts: Delhi Sultanate overall: 1206–1526
Reign lengths are a favourite comparison question
revision_takeaways: Hold the two short dynasties' dates: Khilji 30 years, Sayyid 37 years — the Khilji is shorter.

MPPSC-2017-007.correct_reasoning: Lord Dufferin was Viceroy from 1884 to 1888, and the founding session of the Indian National Congress in December 1885 at Bombay falls inside that window; he even hosted the delegates at the Viceregal Lodge in Calcutta the following year. The Ramakrishna Mission, the Muslim League and the first census all belong to other viceroyalties.

option_explanations.reason: The Ramakrishna Mission was founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897, during Curzon's later decade and after Dufferin had left India.

option_explanations.text: establishment of Muslim League in Dhaka
option_explanations.reason: The All India Muslim League was founded at Dhaka in 1906, under Lord Minto, twenty years after Dufferin's term.
Correct: the Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 while Dufferin was Viceroy.
The first census exercise was conducted in 1871-72 under Mayo and Northbrook, before Dufferin arrived.

key_concepts: INC founded 28 December 1885, Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay
First President: W. C. Bonnerjee; founder-organiser: A. O. Hume
Dufferin was Viceroy 1884–1888
revision_takeaways: 1885 sits inside Dufferin's term: the Congress and the Viceroy are a matched pair.

MPPSC-2017-008.correct_reasoning: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad became Congress President in 1923 at the age of thirty-five, the youngest person to hold the office, and he was elected again in 1940. Jawaharlal Nehru was older at his first presidency in 1929, and Ananda Mohan Bose and Bhupendra Nath Bose led the Congress in the 1890s when both were in their forties or fifties.

option_explanations.reason: Nehru first became Congress President at Lahore in 1929, aged forty, five years older than Azad was in 1923.
Correct: Azad was thirty-five when he became Congress President in 1923, the youngest to hold the post.
Ananda Mohan Bose presided in 1898, in his early fifties, not as a young man.
Bhupendra Nath Bose presided in 1914 at around fifty-seven, well past the age Azad was in 1923.

key_concepts: Azad: Congress President 1923 and 1940; youngest ever
Nehru: 1929 Lahore session, Purna Swaraj
Ananda Mohan Bose: 1898 session, Madras
revision_takeaways: Remember 1923 + 35 years for Azad; it is asked both as a date and as an age.

MPPSC-2017-009.correct_reasoning: The first synchronous, all-India census was held in 1881 under Lord Ripon, and it is treated as the beginning of the regular decennial series that continues today. A census had been attempted in 1872, but it was neither synchronous nor uniform, which is why the question points to 1881.

option_explanations.reason: In 1861 the census consisted of scattered provincial counts taken under different methods and years.
The 1872 exercise was the first attempt at an all-India count but was not synchronous, so it does not begin the regular series.
Correct: 1881 was the first synchronous census, and every ten years since has produced a regular census.
1891 was only the second census of the regular series, so it cannot be the beginning.

key_concepts: First census 1872; first synchronous census 1881
Census conducted every ten years; 2011 was the 15th
Census Commissioner of India, Ministry of Home Affairs
revision_takeaways: Separate the two years: 1872 the attempt, 1881 the regular and scientific start.

MPPSC-2017-010.correct_reasoning: The Second Round Table Conference opened in London in September 1931 with Gandhi as the sole Congress representative, and his party included Mahadev Desai, Pyarelal Nayyar, Sarojini Naidu and Madan Mohan Malaviya. Jawaharlal Nehru was in prison at the time and took no part, which is why he is the name that does not belong to the delegation.

option_explanations.reason: Mahadev Desai was Gandhi's secretary and a member of the Congress delegation at the Second Round Table Conference.
Pyarelal also served as Gandhi's secretary and accompanied him to London for the conference.
Malaviya attended the Second Round Table Conference and spoke on Indian interests in the plenary sessions.
Correct: Nehru was imprisoned during the conference, so he did not participate.

key_concepts: First RTC 1930 (no Congress), Second RTC 1931 (Gandhi), Third RTC 1932
Gandhi-Irwin Pact, March 1931, preceded the second conference
Communal Award and Poona Pact followed the conferences
revision_takeaways: Only the second conference had Gandhi; treat every other name with suspicion.

MPPSC-2017-011.correct_reasoning: The Caspian Sea is ringed by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan, and has no shoreline in Iraq, which lies on the Persian Gulf further south-west. The other three options are genuine Caspian littoral states with ports such as Baku, Anzali and Aktau.

option_explanations.reason: Azerbaijan has a long Caspian coast and its capital Baku is the largest port on the sea.
Iran borders the southern Caspian, with ports at Anzali and Nowshahr.
Correct: Iraq's only coastline is a short stretch of the Persian Gulf, and it does not touch the Caspian Sea.
Kazakhstan holds the longest Caspian shoreline, including the port of Aktau.

key_concepts: Caspian littoral states: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, Azerbaijan
Caspian is a landlocked lake, the largest inland water body
Iraq's coast is on the Persian Gulf, near Basra
revision_takeaways: Five Caspian neighbours, never Iraq: count them clockwise from Russia.

MPPSC-2017-012.correct_reasoning: Kayal is the Malayalam word for the shallow lagoons and backwaters that run parallel to the Kerala coast behind sandbars, as at Vembanad and Ashtamudi. The Terai is a Himalayan foothill belt, the Ganga delta lies in Bengal and the regur is the black cotton soil of the Deccan, so none of them is a kayal.

option_explanations.reason: The Terai is the marshy foothill strip at the base of the Himalayas in Uttar Pradesh and Nepal.
The Ganga delta is the Sundarban region of Bengal, formed by river distributaries rather than coastal lagoons.
Regur is black cotton soil formed from lava, a soil type and not a water body at all.
Correct: kayal denotes Kerala's coastal backwater lagoons, such as Vembanad and Ashtamudi.

key_concepts: Kayal: Kerala backwater lagoon, brackish and parallel to the coast
Vembanad is the largest kayal and hosts the Nehru Trophy boat race
Terai, regur and delta are distinct landform terms
revision_takeaways: Link kayal to Kerala and to the backwater boat races; the word never leaves the Malabar coast.

MPPSC-2017-013.correct_reasoning: The mismatched pair is inselberg with glacier, because an inselberg is an isolated residual hill left standing after long subaerial erosion in arid or semi-arid country, a feature of wind or running water rather than ice. Canyons are cut by rivers, zeugen are shaped by wind, and moraines are deposited by glaciers, so those three pairs are correct.

option_explanations.reason: This pair is right: a canyon is a deep, narrow valley cut by a river, as in the Colorado plateau.
This pair is right: zeugen are table-shaped ridges of resistant rock left by wind abrasion in deserts.
Correct as the mismatch: an inselberg is a residual hill of arid and savanna erosion, not a glacial form.
This pair is right: moraines are the ridges of unsorted debris deposited directly by a glacier.

key_concepts: Inselberg and monadnock: residual hills of the erosion cycle
Zeugen, yardang and mushroom rock are wind-formed
Moraine, drumlin, esker and kame are glacial landforms
revision_takeaways: Arid-zone words (inselberg, zeugen, yardang) never pair with ice.

MPPSC-2017-014.correct_reasoning: Stromboli is a volcanic island north of Sicily whose eruptions have continued almost without pause for centuries, so it is the classic example of an active volcano and gave volcanology the term Strombolian eruption. Dormant and extinct volcanoes show no current activity, and Etna and Vesuvius are its better-known Italian companions.

option_explanations.reason: A dormant volcano is temporarily quiet, whereas Stromboli has erupted repeatedly in recorded history and continues to do so.
Correct: Stromboli is one of the most continuously active volcanoes in the world, with frequent small explosions.
An extinct volcano has no remaining magma supply and will not erupt again, which is not true of Stromboli.
The island is a volcano, so a negative answer is excluded.

key_concepts: Stromboli: Aeolian island, Tyrrhenian Sea, Italy
Strombolian eruption: rhythmic gas-driven explosions
Active, dormant and extinct classify volcanic status
revision_takeaways: The name of the eruption style is the answer: Stromboli is active by definition.

MPPSC-2017-015.correct_reasoning: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted in 1974, and it created the Central and State Pollution Control Boards with powers to set standards and consent to discharges. It was India's first major environmental statute, eight years before the air act and sixteen before the environment protection act.

option_explanations.reason: 1980 is associated with the Forest (Conservation) Act, not with water pollution control.
Correct: the Water Act was passed in 1974 under Article 252 and set up the pollution control boards.
1981 saw the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act; the water law predates it.
The correct year is present among the earlier options, so the negative choice fails.

key_concepts: Water Act 1974; Air Act 1981; Environment Protection Act 1986
CPCB and SPCBs created under the 1974 Act
Water Act passed using Article 252, since water is a state subject
revision_takeaways: Environmental law ladder: water 1974, air 1981, environment 1986.

MPPSC-2017-016.correct_reasoning: The Census of 2011 recorded a population density of 382 persons per square kilometre for India, up from 325 in 2001. Bihar remained the densest state and Arunachal Pradesh the least dense, while Delhi's national capital territory was the densest among the union territories.

option_explanations.reason: Three hundred twenty-five was the density in 2001, the figure this census replaced.
Three hundred thirty-five is close to the 2001 figure but matches no census year.
Correct: the 2011 census gives India a density of 382 persons per square kilometre.
Three hundred eighty-five overshoots the recorded figure and is a near-miss distractor.

key_concepts: Density 2011: 382 per sq km; 2001: 325
Highest state density: Bihar; lowest: Arunachal Pradesh
India's population 2011: 121.09 crore
revision_takeaways: Remember the pair 325 then 382, which also fixes the decade's growth.

MPPSC-2017-017.correct_reasoning: Nathu La is a pass on the Sikkim-China border on the old silk route to Lhasa, not in Arunachal Pradesh, so that pairing is wrong. Lipulekh lies in Uttarakhand, Rohtang in Himachal Pradesh and the Palghat gap in Kerala, and each of those pairs is correct.

option_explanations.reason: This pair is right: Lipulekh pass in Pithoragarh district, Uttarakhand, is a route to the Kailash Mansarovar area.
Correct as the mismatch: Nathu La is in Sikkim, and Arunachal's border passes include Bum La and Diphu.
This pair is right: the Rohtang pass connects Kullu with Lahaul and Spiti in Himachal Pradesh.
This pair is right: the Palghat gap lies between Kerala and Tamil Nadu, with Kerala on its western side.

key_concepts: Nathu La: Sikkim-China, reopened for trade in 2006
Palghat gap divides the Nilgiris from the Annamalai hills
Passes: Lipulekh, Rohtang, Baralacha La, Bomdi La
revision_takeaways: Sikkim owns Nathu La; the Arunachal passes are Bum La and Diphu.

MPPSC-2017-018.correct_reasoning: A peneplain is the nearly level surface produced at the end of Davis's cycle of erosion, when rivers have worn down the land almost to base level, leaving only isolated residual hills. Wind produces pediplains and deflation hollows, groundwater produces karst and glaciers produce cirques, so the river option is the right agent.

option_explanations.reason: Wind erosion produces pediplains, yardangs and deflation basins in deserts, not the peneplain of humid regions.
Groundwater sculpts limestone into karst, with caves, sinkholes and dolines, and cannot plane a whole landscape.
Glacial erosion leaves cirques, arêtes and U-shaped valleys, and the ice retreats before any plain is levelled.
Correct: the peneplain is the end product of long-running water erosion in the normal cycle.

key_concepts: Peneplain: nearly flat surface close to base level
Davis's cycle: youth, maturity, old age
Monadnock: residual hill left on a peneplain
revision_takeaways: Peneplain almost plain, made by rivers; pediplain by wind.

MPPSC-2017-019.correct_reasoning: The Toda are a pastoral community of the Nilgiri Hills in Tamil Nadu, known for their barrel-vaulted huts, buffalo-centred sacred life and the munds that form their settlements. The Jaunsar hills of Uttarakhand, the Garo hills of Meghalaya and the Jaintia hills also host distinctive tribes, but the Toda belong to the Nilgiris.

option_explanations.reason: Jaunsar in Uttarakhand is the home of the Jaunsari and Khasa people, not the Toda.
The Garo hills of Meghalaya are the homeland of the Garo tribe, a matrilineal community.
Correct: the Toda live in the Nilgiri Hills, along with the Kota, Badaga and Kurumba.
The Jaintia hills of Meghalaya are the home of the Pnar or Jaintia people.

key_concepts: Toda: pastoral, buffalo-centred, barrel-vaulted huts
Nilgiri tribal groups: Toda, Kota, Badaga, Kurumba, Irula
Todas are a Scheduled Tribe of Tamil Nadu
revision_takeaways: Toda, Kota, Badaga all sit in the Nilgiris; memorise them as one cluster.

MPPSC-2017-020.correct_reasoning: Ras Tanura, on the Persian Gulf coast of the Eastern Province, is one of the largest oil refineries and export terminals of Saudi Arabia and is operated by Saudi Aramco. Iran, Iraq and the United States all have major refineries, but Ras Tanura is the Saudi facility.

option_explanations.reason: Iran's main refineries are at Abadan, Bandar Abbas and Tehran, not at Ras Tanura.
American refining is concentrated in Texas and Louisiana, at places such as Baytown and Baton Rouge.
Correct: Ras Tanura is Saudi Aramco's largest refinery and crude export terminal on the Gulf.
Iraq's refineries are at Baiji, Basra and Daura, none of them Ras Tanura.

key_concepts: Ras Tanura: Saudi Aramco refinery and export terminal
Abadan: Iran; Baiji: Iraq; Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline
Saudi Arabia is the largest crude exporter
revision_takeaways: Fix Gulf refineries by country: Abadan Iran, Baiji Iraq, Ras Tanura Saudi Arabia.

MPPSC-2017-021.correct_reasoning: Opium is the dried latex of Papaver somniferum, the opium poppy, from which morphine and codeine are extracted. The other botanical names belong to amla, sarpagandha and cinchona, so a single glance at the botanical binomial settles the question.

option_explanations.reason: Emblica officinalis is the Indian gooseberry or amla, a vitamin C rich fruit.
Correct: Papaver somniferum is the opium poppy, the source of opium and its alkaloids.
Rauwolfia serpentina is sarpagandha, the source of reserpine used for blood pressure.
Cinchona species yield quinine, the antimalarial drug.

key_concepts: Papaver somniferum: opium poppy; morphine, codeine, heroin
Cinchona: quinine; Rauwolfia: reserpine
Opium cultivation is licensed in MP, Rajasthan and UP
revision_takeaways: Learn five binomials together: amla, sarpagandha, cinchona, opium poppy, neem.

MPPSC-2017-022.correct_reasoning: The World Health Assembly certified the global eradication of smallpox in May 1980, two years after the last natural case, in Somalia in 1977. Smallpox is the only human disease to have been eradicated by vaccination, and the date marks the success of the intensified WHO campaign begun in 1967.

option_explanations.reason: 1975 was the year the last naturally occurring case was recorded in Asia, in Bangladesh, not the eradication declaration.
Correct: the World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980.
By 1996 smallpox had been gone for sixteen years, and the date belonged to the polio eradication effort.
2008 marked the thirtieth anniversary of eradication and also the year rinderpest was being driven towards eradication.

key_concepts: Last natural case: Somalia, 1977
Eradication declared 1980; vaccine: vaccinia virus
Rinderpest, eradicated in 2011, was the second such disease
revision_takeaways: 1977 last case, 1980 declared: a three-year gap to remember.

MPPSC-2017-023.correct_reasoning: A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria, injecting its genetic material and multiplying inside the cell until it bursts. The word literally means bacterium eater, and phages such as T4 have been central to molecular biology, so the relationship runs from virus to bacterium and not the other way round.

option_explanations.reason: A tailed shape describes the phage's structure, but the organism is a virus, not a bacterium.
New bacterial cells arise by binary fission and are not phages.
The direction is reversed here; viruses are the infectious agent and bacteria the host in this pairing.
Correct: a bacteriophage is a virus whose host is a bacterium.

key_concepts: Lytic and lysogenic cycles of phages
Phage structure: head, tail, tail fibres, DNA
Phage therapy as an alternative to antibiotics
revision_takeaways: Read the suffix as eater: phage eats bacterium, so it is the virus.

MPPSC-2017-024.correct_reasoning: Meiosis is best studied in the anthers because the pollen mother cells there undergo meiosis synchronously and in large numbers, and the anthers are easy to squash and stain. Shoot and root apices divide by mitosis, and leaf cells are mostly differentiated and no longer dividing.

option_explanations.reason: The shoot apex is a meristem where cells divide mitotically to add height, not a site of meiosis.
Root tips also divide by mitosis, supplying cells for root growth.
Correct: pollen mother cells in the anther undergo meiosis, and the anther squashes well for cytology.
Mature leaf cells are differentiated and have stopped dividing, so meiosis cannot be observed there.

key_concepts: Meiosis occurs in spore mother cells of reproductive organs
Microsporogenesis in the anther produces pollen grains
Mitosis in meristems; meiosis in anthers and ovules
revision_takeaways: When the question says meiosis, look for an anther; for mitosis, look for a root tip.

MPPSC-2017-025.correct_reasoning: Sound travels fastest in solids because the particles are packed closely and pass the vibration on quickly, giving a speed of several kilometres per second in steel against about 343 metres per second in air. Liquids and gases slow it down further, and vacuum stops it entirely since there is no medium.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the close packing and strong bonding of solid particles transmit sound fastest, about five kilometres per second in steel.
Liquids transmit sound faster than gases but far slower than solids, around 1,500 metres per second in water.
Gas molecules are far apart, so sound moves at only about 343 metres per second in air.
Sound needs a material medium, and in vacuum there is none, so it does not travel at all.

key_concepts: Speed order: solids more than liquids more than gases
Speed of sound in air about 343 m/s at 20 degrees Celsius
Sound cannot travel in vacuum
revision_takeaways: Denser packing means faster sound; the vacuum option is always the trap.

MPPSC-2017-026.correct_reasoning: The cornea and the lens refract light and the iris and pupil control how much enters, but the actual image is focused on the retina at the back of the eye, where photoreceptors convert it into nerve signals. The image there is real and inverted, and the brain reads it as upright.

option_explanations.reason: The cornea is the transparent front surface that provides most of the eye's refractive power, but no image forms on it.
The iris is the pigmented muscular ring that adjusts the pupil's size, a control mechanism rather than a screen.
The pupil is simply the aperture through which light passes, so nothing is imaged there.
Correct: the lens throws a real, inverted image onto the retina, which carries rods and cones.

key_concepts: Retina holds rods for dim light and cones for colour
Image on the retina is inverted; the brain corrects it
Myopia and hypermetropia are refractive errors
revision_takeaways: Cornea bends, lens focuses, retina receives: only the retina carries the image.

MPPSC-2017-027.correct_reasoning: The kidneys filter blood in the glomeruli of the nephrons and send the waste out as urine through the ureters, bladder and urethra, which is the definition of an excretory organ. Nutrition, transport and respiration are handled by the digestive tract, the circulatory system and the lungs respectively.

option_explanations.reason: Nutrition involves the intake and assimilation of food by the digestive system, not the filtering of blood.
Transport is the job of the heart and blood vessels, which carry substances around the body.
Correct: kidneys remove urea, excess salts and water from the blood and excrete them as urine.
Respiration is gas exchange in the lungs, which is separate from the removal of nitrogenous waste.

key_concepts: Nephron: glomerulus plus tubule, the functional unit
Kidneys also regulate water balance, pH and blood pressure
Excretory system: kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra
revision_takeaways: Kidney equals filtration and urine: the one-word link is excretion.

MPPSC-2017-028.correct_reasoning: Malaria is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Cholera is bacterial, diphtheria is bacterial and pneumonia is caused by bacteria or viruses, so malaria is the only protozoan disease listed.

option_explanations.reason: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae and spreads through contaminated water.
Diphtheria is a bacterial infection of the throat caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or by viruses.
Correct: Plasmodium, a protozoan, causes malaria, and the Anopheles mosquito is its vector.

key_concepts: Plasmodium species: vivax, falciparum, malariae, ovale
Vector: female Anopheles mosquito
Protozoan diseases: malaria, amoebiasis, kala-azar, sleeping sickness
revision_takeaways: Malaria, kala-azar and amoebiasis are the protozoan trio to recall.

MPPSC-2017-029.correct_reasoning: Convection needs a fluid whose heated portion can physically rise and carry the heat with it, so it happens in liquids and gases. Solids have fixed particles that cannot flow and pass heat on by conduction instead, and vacuum has no particles at all, which leaves radiation as the only route.

option_explanations.reason: Solids cannot flow, so the solid half of this pair rules it out; heat moves through them by conduction.
Neither medium supports convection: solids do not flow and vacuum has no matter to carry heat.
Correct: both are fluids, so heated portions rise and cooler portions sink, transferring heat by convection.
Gas convection is real, but vacuum transmits heat only by radiation.

key_concepts: Conduction: solids; convection: fluids; radiation: needs no medium
Sea breeze and land breeze are convection currents
Trade winds and monsoon circulation are large-scale convection
revision_takeaways: Convection is a fluid affair: if there is no flow, there is no convection.

MPPSC-2017-030.correct_reasoning: Vitamins A, B and D were all discovered by Elmer McCollum, while vitamin C was the work of James Lind, who showed in 1747 that citrus fruit cured scurvy. The paper prints the misspelt 'Paul muller' in option D, but the person meant is McCollum, and the pair that breaks is vitamin D with him, since the other two McCollum pairs are right.

option_explanations.reason: This pair is right: McCollum identified vitamin A in 1913 while working on butterfat and cod liver oil.
This pair is also right, since McCollum's research group isolated the B complex vitamins.
Correctly matched: James Lind's 1747 trial with citrus established the antiscorbutic factor, later called vitamin C.
Correct as the mismatch: vitamin D is credited to McCollum, and Paul Muller is remembered for DDT, not a vitamin.

key_concepts: McCollum: vitamins A, B and D
James Lind: scurvy and vitamin C, 1747
Paul Muller: DDT and the 1948 Nobel Prize in Medicine
revision_takeaways: Three vitamins one man, McCollum; vitamin C belongs to Lind and DDT to Muller.

MPPSC-2017-031.correct_reasoning: Lens power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres and is expressed in dioptres, a convex lens having positive power and a concave lens negative. The lumen measures luminous flux, the candela luminous intensity and the 'aeon' is a unit of geological time, so only the dioptre fits the definition.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: power in dioptres equals 1 divided by the focal length in metres.
An aeon is a span of a billion years used in geology and has nothing to do with optics.
The lumen measures luminous flux, the total light output of a source.
The candela is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction, not of lens power.

key_concepts: Power P = 1/f with f in metres; unit dioptre
Convex lens: positive power; concave lens: negative power
Lumen, lux and candela are photometric units
revision_takeaways: Dioptre is per metre: that is why focal length must be converted to metres.

MPPSC-2017-032.correct_reasoning: Graphite is a soft, layer-lattice form of carbon in which the sheets slide over one another easily, which makes it a dry lubricant for locks, bearings and high-temperature use. Cuprite and haematite are copper and iron ores and cryolite is an aluminium smelting flux.

option_explanations.reason: Cuprite is copper(I) oxide, an ore of copper, and it is abrasive rather than slippery.
Correct: the weak forces between graphite's carbon layers let them slide, giving low friction.
Haematite is iron oxide, the main iron ore, and is used for metal extraction rather than for lubrication.
Cryolite, sodium aluminium fluoride, lowers the melting point of alumina in aluminium refining.

key_concepts: Allotropes of carbon: diamond, graphite, fullerene
Graphite: layered hexagonal sheets, conducts electricity
Cryolite used in the Hall-Heroult process
revision_takeaways: Graphite does two jobs in exams: lubricant and electrode.

MPPSC-2017-033.correct_reasoning: Nitrous oxide, N2O, is called laughing gas because short inhalation produces mild euphoria and laughter, and it is still used as an anaesthetic in dentistry and surgery. option_explanations.reason: Fifteen days is the window used for some relief disbursement steps, not for the investigation report.
