Twenty-five days is a distractor close to the correct thirty, with no rule behind it.
Correct: Rule 7 of the 1995 Rules requires the report within thirty days.

key_concepts: Rules 1995: investigation report within 30 days
Relief and rehabilitation duties of the district administration
Trial within two months, appeal to the High Court within 90 days
revision_takeaways: Thirty days for the police report and two months for the trial are the two deadlines to remember.

MPPSC-2017-095.correct_reasoning: The Aitareya Brahmana belongs to the Rigveda, as does the Kaushitaki Brahmana, and it contains the famous Aitareya Upanishad within its later portion. The Gopatha Brahmana belongs to the Atharvaveda, the Shatapatha to the Shukla Yajurveda and the Taittiriya to the Krishna Yajurveda.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the Aitareya Brahmana is attached to the Rigveda and is one of its two surviving Brahmanas.
The Gopatha Brahmana is the only Brahmana of the Atharvaveda.
The Shatapatha Brahmana belongs to the Shukla Yajurveda and contains the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.
The Taittiriya Brahmana is part of the Krishna Yajurveda tradition.

key_concepts: Four Vedas with their Brahmanas and principal Upanishads
Rigveda: Aitareya and Kaushitaki Brahmanas
Samaveda: Tandya and Jaiminiya Brahmanas; Atharvaveda: Gopatha
revision_takeaways: Aitareya is Rigvedic, Shatapatha is Yajurvedic, Gopatha is Atharvan.

MPPSC-2017-096.correct_reasoning: The task force on the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax was headed by Vijay Kelkar, the economist and former Finance Secretary who also chaired the Thirteenth Finance Commission. It recommended a unified destination-based GST with a seamless input tax credit chain, which shaped the 2017 law.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the Kelkar Task Force on GST recommended the tax design that India later adopted.
Montek Singh Ahluwalia, the planner and former Planning Commission deputy chairman, did not head this task force.
Jaitley was the Finance Minister who piloted the GST laws in 2017, not the task force's chairman.
M. Narasimham chaired the banking reform committees, a separate field of work.

key_concepts: GST: 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016; rolled out 1 July 2017
GST Council under Article 279A
Kelkar: Thirteenth Finance Commission, FRBM review and GST design
revision_takeaways: Kelkar means tax reform: FRBM review and the GST task force.

MPPSC-2017-097.correct_reasoning: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976 on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, which followed the 1975 Emergency. Article 51A now lists eleven duties, extended from ten in 2002.

option_explanations.text: At the time of framing of Constitution
option_explanations.reason: The original Constitution of 1950 contained only Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, with no duties chapter.
That date marks the commencement of the Constitution, decades before duties were inserted.
Correct: the 42nd Amendment in 1976 inserted Part IVA, Article 51A.
The 41st Amendment of 1976 dealt with the Election Commission's conditions of service.

key_concepts: Swaran Singh Committee recommended Fundamental Duties
Article 51A: eleven duties, the eleventh added by the 86th Amendment in 2002
Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable
revision_takeaways: 42nd Amendment 1976 gives both Fundamental Duties and the mini-Constitution's other changes.

MPPSC-2017-098.correct_reasoning: Both the Union and the states draw their powers from the Constitution, which distributes them across the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule. The President, the Prime Minister and Parliament all derive their authority from the same document, so none of them can be the source of power.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the Constitution allocates power through the Seventh Schedule and sets limits on it.
The President is himself a creature of the Constitution and exercises only the powers it confers.
The Prime Minister's authority comes from Articles 74 and 75, which are constitutional provisions.
Parliament is not sovereign in India; it legislates within the limits the Constitution sets.

key_concepts: Federalism: distribution of powers between centre and states
Seventh Schedule: Union List 97 entries plus, State List 66 and Concurrent List 47
Parliament's limited sovereignty under a written constitution
revision_takeaways: In India the Constitution is supreme, so every organ's power has that single source.

MPPSC-2017-099.correct_reasoning: A pressure group is an organised body outside the formal structure of government that tries to influence policy, and trade unions are the classic example because they press for wages, safety and labour law. Members of the Lok Sabha, panchayats and the cabinet are part of government itself, not outside pressure groups.

option_explanations.reason: Members of Parliament are inside the legislature, so they are decision makers rather than an outside pressure group.
Elected panchayat members hold constitutional office under Article 243 and are not a pressure group.
The cabinet is the executive government, which pressure groups seek to influence.
Correct: a trade union is an interest group that lobbies government and employers on behalf of workers.

key_concepts: Pressure groups: interest articulation outside parties
Examples: trade unions, FICCI, bar councils, student bodies
Pressure groups versus political parties: contesting elections is the dividing line
revision_takeaways: If the body contests elections it is a party; if it only lobbies, it is a pressure group.

MPPSC-2017-100.correct_reasoning: The International Monetary Fund lends only to its member countries, ordinarily to the member's central bank or finance ministry, so the correct statement is that it grants loans to member countries only. It does not restrict lending to developed countries, nor can it lend to any country regardless of membership.

option_explanations.text: It can grant loans to any country
option_explanations.reason: Non-members cannot borrow, so the word 'any' makes this statement false.

option_explanations.text: It can grant loans to only developed country
option_explanations.reason: The bulk of IMF lending goes to developing members in balance of payments difficulty, so this is the opposite of the truth.

option_explanations.text: It grant loans to member countries only
option_explanations.reason: Correct: membership is the condition for access to IMF resources.

option_explanations.text: It grant loans to the central bank of country
option_explanations.reason: The central bank is normally the counterpart, but this leaves out the membership condition that the question tests.

key_concepts: IMF: 1944 Bretton Woods, 190 members, Washington DC
Quota subscriptions determine voting power and access limits
Structural adjustment conditionality of IMF programmes
revision_takeaways: For IMF statements the deciding word is 'member': membership governs both lending and voting.

MPPSC-2016-001.correct_reasoning: India's longest land border is with Bangladesh, at about 4,097 km, running through West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. China's frontier is the second longest and Pakistan's is shorter still, so the order by length is Bangladesh, China, Pakistan, Nepal.

option_explanations.reason: The India-China boundary runs about 3,488 km across Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal, well short of the Bangladesh figure.
The open India-Nepal border is around 1,751 km, the fourth longest of India's land frontiers.
The Radcliffe Line with Pakistan measures about 3,323 km including the Line of Control, shorter than the eastern border.
Correct: at roughly 4,097 km the Bangladesh border is India's longest, and the enclaves were exchanged in 2015.

key_concepts: Bangladesh 4,097 km; China 3,488 km; Pakistan 3,323 km; Nepal 1,751 km
Total land border about 15,200 km; coastline about 7,516 km
Radcliffe Line 1947; McMahon Line 1914; Durand Line with Afghanistan
revision_takeaways: Rank the land frontiers: Bangladesh, China, Pakistan, Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan, Afghanistan.

MPPSC-2016-002.correct_reasoning: Anai Mudi, also written Anamudi, rises to 2,695 m in the Anaimalai Hills of Kerala and is the highest peak in India south of the Himalayas. Doda Betta is the Nilgiri high point, Guru Shikhar the Aravali high point and Mahendragiri an Eastern Ghats peak, so the tallest of these is in Kerala.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: Anamudi in the Anaimalai Hills of Idukki district is the highest peak of South India at 2,695 m.
Doda Betta at 2,637 m is the highest point of the Nilgiris, second to Anamudi in the south.
Guru Shikhar at 1,722 m is the highest peak of the Aravali, which is a much older, worn-down range.
Mahendragiri in Odisha stands at about 1,501 m and belongs to the Eastern Ghats, far below Anamudi.

key_concepts: Anamudi 2,695 m: highest peak in South India; in Eravikulam National Park
Nilgiri high point Doda Betta; Eastern Ghats high point Arma Konda
Anamudi is nicknamed the Everest of the South
revision_takeaways: Anamudi, Anaimalai, Kerala: one chain to remember for 'highest in the south'.

MPPSC-2016-003.correct_reasoning: The Kashmir Valley is a structural trough bounded on the south-west by the Pir Panjal range and on the north-east by the main Great Himalaya, with the Jhelum draining it. The Zanskar and Ladakh ranges lie further north-east, beyond the Great Himalaya, so they do not enclose the valley.

option_explanations.reason: The Ladakh and Zanskar ranges lie across the Great Himalaya, enclosing the Indus and Zanskar valleys rather than the Kashmir Valley.
Correct: the valley sits between the Pir Panjal to the south-west and the Great Himalaya to the north-east.
Zanskar is beyond the Great Himalaya, so the two ranges named here do not face each other across the valley.
The Karakoram and Ladakh ranges are in the far north, bounding the Nubra and Indus country.

key_concepts: Kashmir Valley: 135 km long, drained by the Jhelum
Pir Panjal: the Lesser Himalaya range, crossed by the Banihal pass
Karewas are lake deposits found on the valley floor
revision_takeaways: Pir Panjal in front, Great Himalaya behind: that pair defines the Kashmir Valley.

MPPSC-2016-004.correct_reasoning: By area the four states rank Rajasthan (342,239 sq km), Maharashtra (307,713), Karnataka (191,791) and Tamil Nadu (130,058), so the descending order is I, III, IV, II. Rajasthan is India's largest state and Madhya Pradesh, which is not in the list, sits between it and Maharashtra.

option_explanations.reason: This puts Tamil Nadu ahead of Maharashtra and Karnataka, which is the wrong way round.
This places Maharashtra above Rajasthan, but Rajasthan is about 34,000 sq km larger.
Correct: Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu is the true descending order of area.
This brings Rajasthan in third, behind two smaller states, so the order is not descending.

key_concepts: Largest states: Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh
Karnataka 191,791 sq km; Tamil Nadu 130,058 sq km
Area ranking differs from population ranking
revision_takeaways: Rajasthan is first in area but only around eighth in population.

MPPSC-2016-005.correct_reasoning: Barren Island is the emergent summit of a volcano in the Andaman Sea and the only confirmed active volcano in India, with eruptions recorded in 1991, 1994-95, 2005 and 2017. The Nicobar and North Andaman islands are part of the same island arc but are not volcanic in origin.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: Barren Island is a volcanic island with a live cone, about 138 km north-east of Port Blair.
Car Nicobar is a flat coral-and-sedimentary island with no volcanic activity.
Little Nicobar is also a non-volcanic island of the Nicobar group, covered in forest and coral terraces.
North Andaman is an uplifted sedimentary island of the Andaman arc, not a volcano.

key_concepts: Barren Island: only active volcano in India, in the Andaman Sea
Narcondam is a dormant volcano in the same arc
Andaman and Nicobar islands lie on the Burma plate margin
revision_takeaways: One volcano in India, and it is Barren: the name does the work.

MPPSC-2016-006.correct_reasoning: The Blue Revolution refers to the rapid growth of aquaculture and fisheries, that is, fish production, so pisciculture is the match. Floriculture is flower farming, sericulture is silk rearing and horticulture is fruit and vegetable cultivation, each with its own colour-coded revolution in exam usage.

option_explanations.reason: Floriculture is the cultivation of flowers and is linked to the ornamental trade, not to the Blue Revolution.
Sericulture is silk production and has its own colour label, the Golden Revolution being used for horticulture and honey.
Correct: pisciculture, or fish farming, is the core of the Blue Revolution in India.
Horticulture is the Golden Revolution, covering fruits, vegetables and flowers.

key_concepts: Blue Revolution: fisheries and aquaculture
Green Revolution: foodgrains; White: milk; Yellow: oilseeds; Pink: prawn and onion
Fish production is a major export earner for India
revision_takeaways: Blue is for water produce, which means fish, which means pisciculture.

MPPSC-2016-007.correct_reasoning: A superimposed boundary is one drawn over an already settled landscape, ignoring the cultural and physical facts on the ground, and the Radcliffe Line of 1947 was drawn in weeks across Punjab and Bengal without regard to communities. An antecedent boundary would predate settlement, a subsequent one would follow it, and a relict boundary is one that has ceased to function.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the Radcliffe Line was imposed on existing populations by an outside commission, the classic superimposed boundary.
An antecedent boundary is drawn before the area is settled, as in parts of the Americas, which is not the Indian case.
A relict boundary no longer functions as a political line, whereas the India-Pakistan border is very much in force.
A subsequent boundary is drawn after settlement and follows cultural differences, which the Radcliffe Line deliberately did not do.

key_concepts: Boundary types by timing: antecedent, subsequent, superimposed, relict
Radcliffe Line: 17 August 1947 award, drawn by Cyril Radcliffe
Africa's colonial boundaries are the standard example of superimposed lines
revision_takeaways: Drawn over people by outsiders equals superimposed; the Radcliffe Line is the textbook case.

MPPSC-2016-008.correct_reasoning: Cyclone Hudhud came in from the Bay of Bengal and made landfall near Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014, devastating the north Andhra coast before weakening over Chhattisgarh. Its name was contributed by Oman, and the response in Andhra Pradesh became a benchmark for evacuation.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: Hudhud struck near Visakhapatnam in October 2014 with winds above 170 km per hour.
Kerala lies on the Arabian Sea side and Hudhud never crossed the peninsula to reach it.
Chennai was hit by the 2015 floods and by cyclone Vardah in 2016, not by Hudhud.
West Bengal's storms include Aila and Amphan; Hudhud made landfall far to the south-west.

key_concepts: Bay of Bengal cyclones: Hudhud 2014, Phailin 2013, Amphan 2020
Landfall categories use wind speed; storm surge causes most deaths
Cyclone names come from a rotating list of member countries
revision_takeaways: Hudhud means hoopoe and hit Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, in October 2014.

MPPSC-2016-009.correct_reasoning: Rana Pratap Sagar is the dam and reservoir at Rawatbhata on the Chambal, downstream of Gandhi Sagar and upstream of Jawahar Sagar, and it is part of the Gandhi Sagar-Chambal cascade. Nagarjuna Sagar is on the Krishna, Rihand on the Rihand river and Vindhya Sagar is a small MP tank, none of them on the Chambal.

option_explanations.reason: Nagarjuna Sagar stands on the Krishna river in Telangana, one of the earliest large masonry dams of India.
Correct: the dam at Rawatbhata on the Chambal forms the Rana Pratap Sagar reservoir and has a hydropower station.
Vindhya Sagar is a small state reservoir of Madhya Pradesh, not one of the Chambal dams.
Rihand is a reservoir on the Rihand river, a Son tributary, in Uttar Pradesh.

key_concepts: Chambal cascade: Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar, Kota Barrage
Rana Pratap Sagar is famous for the Rawatbhata atomic power station nearby
Chambal drains the Malwa plateau into the Yamuna
revision_takeaways: Four Chambal dams in order, with Rana Pratap Sagar at Rawatbhata.

MPPSC-2016-010.correct_reasoning: Cochin Shipyard Limited is the largest shipbuilding and repair facility in India, a public sector yard that also built the Vikrant's hull and repairs the Navy's carriers. Kolkata's Garden Reach and Visakhapatnam's Hindustan Shipyard are significant but smaller, and Mumbai's yards serve port needs.

option_explanations.reason: Kolkata has the Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers, a major yard but not the largest by capacity.
Correct: Cochin Shipyard is India's largest shipbuilding and maintenance facility, at Kochi in Kerala.
Mumbai's yards are mainly repair docks, including the Mazagon Dock, which is known for submarines rather than size.
Hindustan Shipyard at Visakhapatnam is one of the oldest yards but smaller than Cochin in capacity.

key_concepts: Cochin Shipyard: largest Indian yard, public sector, under the Ministry of Shipping
Mazagon Dock builds submarines; Garden Reach builds warships
Shipbuilding is covered under the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy
revision_takeaways: Largest shipyard is Cochin, and the second name to know is Garden Reach.

MPPSC-2016-011.correct_reasoning: Manikaran lies in the Parvati Valley of Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh, where hot springs are tapped for a small geothermal power plant. The site is also a place of pilgrimage, and the state's geothermal belt runs along the Beas and Parvati valleys.

option_explanations.reason: Arunachal has hot springs at Tawang and Dirang, but its geothermal potential is still exploratory.
Jammu and Kashmir's springs at Puga in Ladakh are promising but Manikaran is far away in Himachal.
Correct: the experimental 5 MW plant at Manikaran is in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district.
Uttarakhand has Tapovan and Badrinath springs, but not the Manikaran plant.

key_concepts: Geothermal energy: heat from the earth's interior used to raise steam
Manikaran hot springs, Parvati Valley, Kullu
Puga in Ladakh is India's most promising geothermal field
revision_takeaways: Manikaran, Kullu, Himachal Pradesh: the Indian geothermal example.

MPPSC-2016-012.correct_reasoning: The badlands and ravines of the Chambal in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan are cut by deep gullies that retreat headward into soft alluvium, so gully erosion is the process. Sheet erosion removes a thin uniform layer, overgrazing is a contributory cause rather than the mechanism, and wind erosion shapes deserts.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: concentrated runoff carves deep gullies whose headward retreat produces the Chambal ravine badlands.
Sheet erosion strips soil evenly across a slope and does not cut the deep branching channels seen at Chambal.
Overgrazing removes protective vegetation and accelerates erosion, but it is a cause of vulnerability, not the landform process.
Wind erosion dominates arid Rajasthan further west and forms dunes, not the dendritic ravines of the Chambal.

key_concepts: Badland: intensely dissected land unusable for farming
Gully erosion follows uncontrolled runoff on soft, easily erodible alluvium
Chambal ravines are a classic Indian example alongside the Yamuna ravines
revision_takeaways: Ravines are gullies grown up, and the agent is running water.

MPPSC-2016-013.correct_reasoning: The Central Ganga Authority, later the National Ganga River Basin Authority, was set up in February 1985 to implement the Ganga Action Plan under the Environment Protection Act framework, chaired by the Prime Minister. The 1986 environment law and the 2009 NGRBA are separate, later steps.

option_explanations.reason: 1998 belongs to later river conservation programmes, not the founding of the Ganga authority.
1972 is the year of the Wildlife (Protection) Act and the Stockholm Conference, not the Ganga authority.
2001 is far too late for the body that launched the Ganga Action Plan in 1985.
Correct: the Central Ganga Authority was constituted in 1985 under Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi.

key_concepts: Ganga Action Plan 1985, Phase I and II
NGRBA 2009, chaired by the Prime Minister; Namami Gange launched in 2014
River pollution control is shared between the centre and states
revision_takeaways: Ganga Authority 1985 comes just before the Environment Protection Act of 1986.

MPPSC-2016-014.correct_reasoning: The Silent Valley is a tropical evergreen rainforest in the Palakkad district of Kerala, and the hydroelectric project proposed there in the 1970s was dropped after a national campaign led by the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad. The valley is now a national park and part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve.

option_explanations.reason: Uttarakhand's environmental battles were over the Tehri dam and limestone quarrying, not Silent Valley.
Himachal's controversies centred on hydro projects in the Sutlej valley and on the Great Himalayan National Park.
Correct: Silent Valley in Palakkad district, Kerala, was saved from a hydroelectric project and became a national park.
Tamil Nadu's forests host the Mudumalai sanctuary, but Silent Valley lies across the state border in Kerala.

key_concepts: Silent Valley National Park, Palakkad, Kerala
Saved in 1983 after the Silent Valley Hydro-Electric Project was abandoned
Habitat of the lion-tailed macaque
revision_takeaways: Silent Valley equals Kerala, lion-tailed macaques and a cancelled dam.

MPPSC-2016-015.correct_reasoning: The Golden Quadrilateral connects the four metropolitan cities Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata in a loop of about 5,846 km, built under the National Highways Development Project. The other options describe north-south or east-west corridors or simply different routes.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: these four metros form the Golden Quadrilateral, the country's first mega highway project.
This is a stretch of the North-South Corridor, a different NHDP programme.
Srinagar to Kolkata is the northern arm of the East-West Corridor, not the quadrilateral.
Porbandar to Kolkata belongs to the East-West Corridor, connecting Gujarat with Bengal.

key_concepts: Golden Quadrilateral: 5,846 km, launched 2001 under NHDP Phase I
North-South Corridor: Srinagar to Kanyakumari; East-West: Porbandar to Silchar
Golden Quadrilateral connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata
revision_takeaways: Four metros in a loop is the Quadrilateral; the corridors run north-south and east-west.

MPPSC-2016-016.correct_reasoning: The potato is a modified underground stem, specifically a tuber, because it carries axillary buds in the depressions called eyes and stores starch. Roots bear no buds, bulbs are made of fleshy leaf scales as in onion, and a fruit is the ripened ovary of a flower.

option_explanations.reason: A root has no nodes or buds; the potato's eyes are buds, which shows it is stem tissue.
A fruit develops from the ovary after flowering, whereas the potato is a vegetative storage organ.
Correct: the potato is a stem tuber, a swollen underground stem with nodes and buds.
A bulb, as in onion and garlic, is a short stem surrounded by fleshy scale leaves, which the potato is not.

key_concepts: Stem modifications: tuber, rhizome, corm, bulb
Eyes of the potato are axillary buds used for seed propagation
Solanum tuberosum belongs to the Solanaceae family
revision_takeaways: Bud-bearing underground swelling means stem: potato is a tuber, onion is a bulb.

MPPSC-2016-017.correct_reasoning: Helium belongs to group 18 of the periodic table, the noble gases, which are characterised by full outer shells and very low reactivity. Hydrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide are not noble gases, even though hydrogen sits next to helium in the first period.

option_explanations.reason: Hydrogen has one electron and forms compounds readily; despite its position it is not a noble gas.
Oxygen is a highly reactive group 16 element and the basis of combustion.
Correct: helium is a noble gas with a closed 1s2 shell, the least reactive element known.
Carbon dioxide is a compound, not an element, so it cannot be a noble gas.

key_concepts: Noble gases: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon
Full valence shells make noble gases chemically inert
Helium is used in balloons and cryogenics
revision_takeaways: Group 18 is the noble family, and helium is its lightest member.

MPPSC-2016-018.correct_reasoning: The liver is the largest gland in the human body, weighing about 1.5 kg in an adult, and it secretes bile, stores glycogen and detoxifies the blood. The pancreas and salivary glands are much smaller, and the adrenal glands are small endocrine caps on the kidneys.

option_explanations.reason: The pancreas has both digestive and hormonal roles but weighs only about 80 to 100 grams.
Correct: at about 1.5 kg the liver is the largest gland and the largest internal organ.
Salivary glands are small paired glands that secrete saliva into the mouth.
The adrenal glands are tiny caps on top of the kidneys that release adrenaline and cortisol.

key_concepts: Liver: bile secretion, glycogen storage, detoxification
Largest organ is the skin; largest gland is the liver
The liver receives blood through the portal vein
revision_takeaways: Skin is the largest organ, liver the largest gland: keep the two apart.

MPPSC-2016-019.correct_reasoning: All mammals breathe through lungs, even the whales and dolphins that live in water, since their lungs are supplied by a diaphragm-driven system. Gills belong to fish, the tracheal system to insects, and skin respiration supplements rather than replaces lungs in most mammals.

option_explanations.reason: Gills extract dissolved oxygen from water and are the breathing organs of fish, not of mammals.
Insects breathe through a network of tracheae opening at spiracles, a system mammals do not have.
Skin respiration matters in amphibians and earthworms and only supplementarily in mammals.
Correct: mammals, including aquatic ones, breathe air with lungs.

key_concepts: Respiratory organs: lungs in mammals, gills in fish, tracheae in insects, skin in earthworms
Alveoli provide the surface for gas exchange in mammalian lungs
The diaphragm is unique to mammals
revision_takeaways: Whales breathe air with lungs, which is why the 'lungs' answer covers all mammals.

MPPSC-2016-020.correct_reasoning: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid, roughly 5 per cent, produced by fermenting ethanol with Acetobacter bacteria, so acetic acid is its chemical identity. Butyric acid smells of rancid butter, formic acid is the ant-sting acid and tartaric acid occurs in grapes and tamarind.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: vinegar is ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH3COOH, in water.
Butyric acid gives rancid butter its smell and appears in the digestive tract, not in vinegar.
Formic acid is methanoic acid, found in ant stings and insect venom.
Tartaric acid is the main acid of grapes and tamarind, and it appears in baking powder.

key_concepts: Acetic acid CH3COOH is a weak carboxylic acid
Fermentation: sugar to ethanol to acetic acid
Useful acids: citric (lemon), lactic (curd), oxalic (tomato)
revision_takeaways: Vinegar equals acetic acid, and the everyday acids each have a fixed source.

MPPSC-2016-021.correct_reasoning: Myopia, or short-sightedness, is an eye defect in which the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina, so distant objects look blurred and a concave lens is used to correct it. It has no link with the heart, ear or kidney.

option_explanations.reason: Cardiac disorders include hypertension and arrhythmia; myopia is a refractive error of the eye.
Ear disorders affect hearing and balance, such as tinnitus or vertigo.
Correct: myopia is poor distant vision caused by an over-long eyeball or too much lens curvature.
Kidney disease affects filtration and blood pressure, not the refraction of light.

key_concepts: Myopia: image before the retina, corrected with a concave lens
Hypermetropia: image behind the retina, corrected with a convex lens
Presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation
revision_takeaways: Myopia is short sight and needs a concave lens; the organ is always the eye.

MPPSC-2016-022.correct_reasoning: Heat is measured in calories and joules, and the kilocalorie and kilojoule are simply multiples of them. The watt is a joule per second, that is, a unit of power, so it does not measure heat quantity.

option_explanations.reason: A calorie is the classic unit of heat, the energy needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 degree Celsius.
The kilocalorie is 1,000 calories and is the unit used on food labels for energy content.
The kilojoule is the SI-based multiple of the joule, which is itself the SI unit of energy and heat.
Correct as the odd one out: a watt is one joule per second, a rate of energy transfer, so it measures power.

key_concepts: 1 calorie = 4.18 joules
Power = energy per unit time; watt = J/s
Electric heaters are rated in watts because they are power devices
revision_takeaways: Joules and calories are energy; watts are energy per second.

MPPSC-2016-023.correct_reasoning: A simple barometer uses mercury because its high density of 13.6 g per cc keeps the column to about 76 cm at sea level; water would need a tube over 10 m tall and alcohol still higher. That is why mercury is the standard liquid in barometers and manometers.

option_explanations.reason: Water is too light: atmospheric pressure would support a column of more than 10 metres, which is impractical.
Correct: mercury's density allows a manageable 76 cm column, and it does not wet the glass.
Alcohol is less dense than water and also evaporates, so it suits thermometers, not barometers.
Only mercury is used in practice, so a blanket 'all' answer is wrong.

key_concepts: Atmospheric pressure at sea level equals 760 mm of mercury or 101.3 kPa
Mercury barometer, aneroid barometer, altimeter
Torricelli's experiment established the principle in 1643
revision_takeaways: Density is the reason: mercury compresses the column to 76 cm.

MPPSC-2016-024.correct_reasoning: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels formed from buried organic matter over millions of years. Uranium is a radioactive metal mined from rock and used as nuclear fuel, so it is not a fossil fuel.

option_explanations.reason: Coal is compressed plant remains and is the classic fossil fuel.
Petroleum forms from marine organic matter and is refined into petrol, diesel and kerosene.
Natural gas is mostly methane formed alongside oil and coal beds.
Correct: uranium is nuclear fuel obtained by mining and enrichment, not a fossil fuel, though it is also non-renewable.

key_concepts: Fossil fuels are carbon-based remains of ancient life
Uranium-235 undergoes fission in reactors
Both fossil and nuclear fuels are non-renewable, but only the first are fossil
revision_takeaways: Uranium is non-renewable and non-fossil; that distinction is the answer.

MPPSC-2015-021.correct_reasoning: Alfalfa is Medicago sativa, a deep-rooted legume grown as fodder and called lucerne in India, valued for its protein and its ability to fix nitrogen. Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen through rhizobia
Alfalfa is rich in protein, calcium and vitamins A, C, E and K

MPPSC-2015-022.correct_reasoning: Chlorofluorocarbons release chlorine in the stratosphere, where each chlorine atom catalyses the destruction of thousands of ozone molecules, which is why they are the pollutants that damage the ozone layer most. Ozone depletion differs from global warming but shares some causes

MPPSC-2015-023.correct_reasoning: The roaring forties, furious fifties and shrieking sixties are the strong westerly winds of the southern hemisphere between about 40 and 70 degrees south, where open ocean allows them to blow unimpeded. The Southern Ocean's uninterrupted fetch makes these winds strong

MPPSC-2015-024.correct_reasoning: Santos, the port city of Sao Paulo state, is the world's leading coffee export port because the Brazilian coffee belt drains through it. MPPSC-2015-025.correct_reasoning: An isohyet joins places of equal rainfall, just as an isobar joins equal pressure points, an isotherm equal temperature and an isohaline equal salinity. The prefix 'hyet' comes from the Greek word for rain, which is what distinguishes it from the other isopleths.

Isohyets map rainfall distribution and reveal rain-shadow areas
Isobars and isotherms appear on weather charts
revision_takeaways: Rainfall line is an isohyet; salinity line an isohaline.

MPPSC-2015-026.correct_reasoning: The Bhagirathi, rising at Gangotri, and the Alaknanda, rising near Badrinath, join at Dev Prayag in Uttarakhand, and from that confluence the river is called the Ganga. MPPSC-2015-027.correct_reasoning: Sabarimala, the hill shrine of Ayyappa in the Western Ghats of Pathanamthitta district, lies in Kerala and draws pilgrims from across south India. The temple is reached through Kerala's own roads and towns, and it is not in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu or Karnataka.

MPPSC-2015-028.correct_reasoning: Sikkim is wedged between Nepal to the west, Bhutan to the east and China to the north, which makes it the only Indian state with three international neighbours. MPPSC-2015-029.correct_reasoning: Bailadila in Dantewada district of Chhattisgarh is one of India's richest iron-ore deposits, supplying high-grade haematite to steel plants and to the Visakhapatnam port for export. MPPSC-2015-031.correct_reasoning: Talcher, in Angul district of Odisha, is one of India's largest coalfields and feeds thermal power stations and the Talcher fertiliser plant. MPPSC-2015-032.correct_reasoning: The Human Development Index combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life measured by life expectancy, knowledge measured by mean and expected years of schooling, and a decent standard of living measured by gross national income per capita. MPPSC-2015-033.correct_reasoning: The Fifth Five-Year Plan, running from 1974 to 1979, carried the slogan garibi hatao and set the removal of poverty and the attainment of self-reliance as its objectives. MPPSC-2015-034.correct_reasoning: The Second Five-Year Plan, 1956-61, was built on the Mahalanobis model, which stressed heavy industry and capital goods so that the economy could produce machines for its own future growth. MPPSC-2015-035.correct_reasoning: The first general election under the new Constitution was held between October 1951 and February 1952 for the Lok Sabha and most state assemblies, and the first Lok Sabha met in May 1952. 1950 is the year the Constitution came into force, and 1949 its adoption, so neither can be the election year.

MPPSC-2015-036.correct_reasoning: B.R. MPPSC-2015-050.correct_reasoning: The Dead Sea has the highest salinity of any large water body, around 34 per cent, because it is an enclosed basin in a hot desert with no outlet, so water leaves only by evaporation and salts accumulate. option_explanations.reason: Correct: Junko Tabei, spelled here as Taibei, was the first woman on Everest.
No climber of this name holds the first-woman record.
Tereshkova was the first woman in space, in 1963, not on Everest.

Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary summited Everest in 1953
Bachendri Pal was the first Indian woman on Everest, in 1984
revision_takeaways: First woman on Everest: Junko Tabei of Japan, 1975.

MPPSC-2015-091.correct_reasoning: A fathometer measures ocean depth by sending a sound pulse to the seabed and timing its echo, which is why it is also called an echo sounder. Barometers measure pressure, rain gauges measure rainfall and sound-level meters measure intensity, so depth is the only fitting use.

option_explanations.reason: Earthquakes are recorded by a seismograph.
Rainfall is measured by a rain gauge or pluviometer.
Correct: a fathometer measures sea depth by echo sounding.
Sound intensity is measured in decibels by a sound-level meter.

key_concepts: Fathom: a nautical unit of depth, about 1.8 m
Echo sounding uses the speed of sound in water
Bathymetry maps ocean floor relief
revision_takeaways: Fathometer equals ocean depth.

MPPSC-2015-092.correct_reasoning: The Tropical Forest Research Institute at Jabalpur, a unit of the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education, is the regional forest research centre for central India, which makes Jabalpur the answer. MPPSC-2015-093.correct_reasoning: A microscope is used to study objects that are too small to be seen with the naked eye and that are placed close to the lens, so the paper's phrasing 'micro and nearby objects' captures both features. A telescope, by contrast, is for distant objects, which is why the distant and merely nearby options are wrong.

option_explanations.reason: Distant objects are the province of the telescope, not the microscope.
Being nearby is necessary but not sufficient; the object must also be very small.

key_concepts: Microscope: magnification of small specimens
Telescope: distant objects; microscope: near and minute objects
Compound microscope uses objective and eyepiece lenses
revision_takeaways: Microscope studies micro, nearby specimens.

MPPSC-2015-094.correct_reasoning: A person with blood group O has no A or B antigens on the red cells, so the blood can be given to recipients of any ABO group, which makes O the universal donor. AB is the universal recipient, while A and B can donate only to compatible groups.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: group O lacks A and B antigens and is the universal donor.
Group A blood carries the A antigen and cannot be given to group B or O recipients.
Group B blood carries the B antigen and is incompatible with A and O recipients.
AB is the universal recipient, not the universal donor.

key_concepts: ABO system: antigens A and B, antibodies in plasma
O negative is the universal red-cell donor
AB positive is the universal recipient
revision_takeaways: Universal donor is O; universal recipient is AB.

MPPSC-2015-095.correct_reasoning: A lactometer measures the density and purity of milk, working on the same floatation principle as a hydrometer, and adulteration with water shows up as a lower reading. A barometer measures pressure and a hygrometer measures humidity, so neither applies to milk.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: a lactometer tests milk density and detects added water.
A hydrometer measures the density of liquids generally, and the milk-specific instrument is the lactometer.
A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
A hygrometer measures humidity in the air.

key_concepts: Lactometer: milk density, calibrated in lactometer degrees
Normal milk density about 1.026 to 1.032 g per ml
Fat and SNF tests accompany density testing in dairies
revision_takeaways: Milk density is tested with a lactometer.

MPPSC-2015-096.correct_reasoning: A seismograph records the ground motion produced by an earthquake and from that record the magnitude and intensity are worked out. A barometer measures pressure, a hydrometer measures liquid density and a polygraph records physiological responses, so the seismograph is the only instrument for earthquakes.

option_explanations.reason: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, used in weather work.
A hydrometer measures the density of liquids.
A polygraph records pulse, breathing and skin response in interrogation.
Correct: a seismograph records earthquake waves.

key_concepts: Richter scale: magnitude; Mercalli scale: intensity
Seismograph consists of a seismometer and a recorder
Focus and epicentre describe an earthquake's location
revision_takeaways: Earthquake intensity is read from a seismograph.

MPPSC-2015-097.correct_reasoning: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when a mould of Penicillium notatum inhibited the growth of bacteria on a culture plate, an observation that opened the antibiotic era. option_explanations.reason: Correct: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Roentgen in 1895.
Streptomycin was isolated by Selman Waksman and Albert Schatz in 1943.
The telephone is attributed to Alexander Graham Bell, in 1876.

key_concepts: Penicillin: first antibiotic, Fleming 1928, purified by Florey and Chain
Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Florey and Chain
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses
revision_takeaways: Fleming equals penicillin; Roentgen equals X-rays.

MPPSC-2015-098.correct_reasoning: In the northern hemisphere the longest day is the summer solstice on 21 June, when the sun's rays fall vertically on the Tropic of Cancer and the north pole is tilted towards the sun. 22 December is the shortest day there, and the May and December dates in the options do not mark a solstice.

option_explanations.reason: 21 May is a month before the solstice and not the longest day.

Equinoxes on 21 March and 23 September
Day length varies with latitude and axial tilt
revision_takeaways: Longest day in India: 21 June, the summer solstice.
